morningLine: Radio Shack enters the compatible contest; home computers draw, dial and shop.

lead.headline: Tandy brings a $1,199 IBM-compatible into Radio Shack
lead.dek: The Tandy 1000 combines PC-compatible work with color, sound and bundled DeskMate applications.
body: Radio Shack has a new contender for the home and small-office desk this week. The Tandy 1000 enters the IBM-compatible contest at an advertised $1,199 for the original 128K machine with a 360K floppy drive. A monitor is extra: the headline price is not a complete color-display system.

The attraction is not simply a lower-priced business box. Built-in monochrome and color graphics support, PCjr-compatible color capabilities and three-voice sound give the machine a foothold in home entertainment as well as office work. Connection to a television calls for an optional RF modulator. Buyers should distinguish these included capabilities from the accessories needed to use them.

DeskMate comes with the computer. Its TEXT, WORKSHEET, FILER, TELECOM, CALENDAR and MAIL applications offer a ready starting point for letters, figures, records and communication. The telephone side still needs a modem; Radio Shack advertises a 300-baud modem board at $179.95 rather than including one in the base package.

Tandy also advertises a 256K, color-monitor configuration at $2,048.90 and compares it with an IBM PC configuration costing more than $3,100. That is the manufacturer’s own comparison, not an independent equivalence test. Expansion toward 640K and an advertised $299.95 memory board make the upgrade budget another part of the buying decision.

stories.headline: The bulletin board becomes a neighborhood without boundaries
body: November’s COMPUTE! describes a neighborhood reached through the telephone line. Hobby bulletin boards carry messages, technical advice, classified advertisements and public-domain software. Most serve one caller at a time, putting a busy signal between the newcomer and the conversation.

Chicago programmer John Semenek recalls finding only one local Atari board when he began looking; the report now counts at least 20. Stan and Susie Subeck’s Valley Girl BBS adds adventure games and a trivia quiz to its Atari-based service. Games on a modem line are already part of the local scene, even when only one player can call at a time.

The unpaid work is considerable. A survey by Plumb editor Ric Manning puts average setup above $3,000, another $50 in monthly expense and chores at up to 50 hours a month. Kent Fillmore’s Apple II-based Draco-Net suggests a larger ambition through a proposed franchise network. The proposal is not yet a completed nationwide service.

stories.headline: Shopping from the keyboard enters the living room
body: The home computer is acquiring a shopping counter. Selby Bateman’s November COMPUTE! survey describes CompuServe’s Electronic Mall, Comp-U-Store, Chemical Bank Pronto and Chicago Keyfax as parts of the growing online-service landscape.

CompuServe’s Mall stays open 24 hours a day, supplying product descriptions, shipping information, order forms and a mailbox for merchant questions. The practical test is whether finding and comparing goods through a terminal is worth the time and connection cost. Analyst Gary Arlen cautions that it is not as easy as flipping through catalog pages.

Viewtron in Miami offers another approach, using a dedicated $600 AT&T Sceptre terminal rather than an ordinary home computer. American People/Link is meanwhile scheduled for December, with mail, party-line communication, bulletin boards and games among its plans. A promised service should not be confused with one already taking calls.

stories.headline: KoalaPad gives the PCjr a drawing surface
body: PCjr owners can put a drawing surface beside the keyboard. Lee Noel’s November COMPUTE! review examines the KoalaPad and KoalaPainter package, requiring a 128K PCjr, disk drive, DOS 2.1 and color display. The tablet connects through a joystick port.

The roughly six-by-eight-inch unit contains a pressure-sensitive drawing area about four inches square. Icon menus, eight brush styles, zoom, straight-line tools and mirrored drawing provide a broad set of ways to build a picture. KoalaPainter works at 160 by 200 pixels with 16 colors; halftone mixtures suggest additional shades without adding hardware colors.

Noel questions the low-resolution choice when PCjr can also offer 320 by 200 with 16 colors. Koala cites memory conservation and clarity on televisions and composite monitors. Another limitation is hardcopy: the package has no built-in printing, leaving saved disks, photographs or videotape as the documented ways to preserve the artwork.

stories.headline: WizType turns typing practice into a cartoon duel
body: Sierra’s WizType makes typing practice a contest with the Wizard of Id. James V. Trunzo’s November COMPUTE! review covers the Atari version and lists Apple II-family and Commodore 64 editions as well. At least 32K and a disk drive are required; the review price is $34.95.

Correct typing lets the Wizard subdue the spirit, while mistakes allow it to become a fire-breathing dragon. Game, Drill, Practice, Words, Own Lesson and Paragraphs modes give the cartoon contest a more conventional teaching foundation. Drill speeds range from 10 to 60 words per minute.

The Paragraphs menu includes eight literary works, with selections from Hamlet, A Tale of Two Cities, the Gettysburg Address and Mother Goose. Custom lessons let the typist supply other material. This is a November review of an available program, not evidence of a release during this particular week.

computerItems.title: Commodore Plus/4 and C64 are not ROM-swappable upgrades
computerItems.summary: November COMPUTE! answers Ken Climer: ROMs physically/electrically fit but their software is incompatible with C64 memory, graphics, sound and I/O mapping.

softwareList.name: DeskMate
softwareList.detail: Bundled with original Tandy 1000; TEXT, WORKSHEET, FILER, TELECOM, CALENDAR and MAIL. Hardware modem required for telephone communication.

softwareList.name: OmniWriter & OmniSpell
softwareList.detail: Joseph R. Sutton’s C64 review lists HES package at $59.95. Mail merge accepts standard Commodore sequential files; spell checker includes user dictionary and word lists. Reviewer objects to manual page breaks and absent RS-232 printer support.

worldAnchor.headline: Reagan wins re-election
worldAnchor.summary: In the November 6 election, Ronald Reagan and George Bush carry 49 states; Walter Mondale and Geraldine Ferraro win Minnesota and the District of Columbia.

bbsNote.headline: Atari games and local communities move onto BBS lines
bbsNote.summary: November COMPUTE! reports local boards, operator costs and 300/1200-bps choices; these desk notes summarize contemporary reporting.

posts.text: Stan and Susie Subeck offer adventure games and a trivia quiz; single-user connections and disk capacity constrain service.
Reported average setup exceeds $3,000, with $50 monthly expense and as much as 50 hours of maintenance.
Jerry Hussong argues that local social boards still justify 300 bps; 1200 bps makes greater economic sense for large transfers and toll calls.
Commercial services offer shopping or banking; richer Viewtron graphics require a dedicated $600 Sceptre terminal.

curiosity.headline: A Valley Girl bulletin board says “de-val” instead of goodbye
curiosity.summary: The Subeck family’s Atari board translates computer commands into Valley Girl jargon.
curiosity.detail: Kathy Yakal reports that their 13-year-old daughter’s speech inspired the theme: users “bag” messages rather than delete them and “de-val” rather than exit. It is also an educational project for their 12- and 13-year-old children, who help maintain the board. This is a same-month feature, not a launch dated to this week.
